question: How can the frequency generation of sinusoidal implicit neural representations be characterized well enough to initialize them robustly and keep their learned spectrum within a desired bandlimit?

key_findings.claim: A hidden sinusoidal neuron admits an amplitude-phase expansion whose frequencies are integer combinations of first-layer frequencies.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 expresses a three-layer hidden neuron as an infinite sum of sinusoids; Bessel-function products of hidden weights set amplitudes, while first-layer frequencies set the generated frequency lattice.

key_findings.claim: The amplitude bound motivates direct control of hidden weights as a soft spectral filter.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 bounds each generated harmonic's amplitude using the corresponding hidden-weight row and factorial terms; clamping or tanh-bounding columns suppresses large multiples of high input frequencies.

key_findings.claim: TUNER initializes a dense set of low integer frequencies and a sparse grid of high frequencies so small integer combinations can fill the target spectrum.
key_findings.evidence: The method freezes periodic first-layer frequencies, reserves about 70% for a low-frequency region, spreads the remainder over the high-frequency region, and includes coordinate unit frequencies to avoid sub-periods.

key_findings.claim: On Kodak image fitting, bounding improves unsupervised derivative fidelity much more than signal PSNR, consistent with suppressing high-frequency overfit.
key_findings.evidence: Across the reported settings, fixed bounds increase average gradient PSNR by 9.6 dB and improve signal PSNR; a 512-square example changes from 30.8/15.8 dB signal/gradient to 35.1/27.8 dB.

key_findings.claim: TUNER is more robust than SIREN to a high or misspecified bandlimit and compares favorably with BACON and BANF on the tested images.
key_findings.evidence: Sweeps over network shapes and bandlimits show SIREN degrading sharply as the frequency threshold grows, while TUNER maintains better signal and gradient PSNR; visual comparisons report less ringing than BACON and clearer filtering than BANF.

key_findings.claim: The theoretical spectrum is an infinite expansion, so practical bandlimiting is amplitude suppression rather than literal removal of all out-of-band terms.
key_findings.evidence: The bound makes amplitudes decay as integer coefficients grow, and the paper describes TUNER as a soft filter; finite thresholds and optimization do not create a compactly supported Fourier transform in the strict sense.

method.core_idea: Derive the Fourier-like expansion of composed sine layers, then use its frequency and amplitude structure to design first-layer sampling and hidden-weight constraints.
method.mechanism: Frozen integer input frequencies determine the frequency lattice. Dense low-frequency sampling enables local combinations; sparse high-frequency sampling covers the band. Fixed clamps or trainable tanh-scaled column bounds regularize the amplitude of generated high-frequency combinations.
assumptions: Signals are represented on a periodicized low-dimensional domain with a known or conservatively chosen Nyquist limit.
Integer first-layer frequencies are an appropriate basis for the target.
Three-layer sinusoidal MLP analysis captures the important behavior of the tested networks.
Analytical image gradients compared with Sobel gradients are a useful proxy for out-of-sample smoothness.
Restricting hidden weights does not remove target frequencies needed for reconstruction.

techniques.role: Decomposes composed sine neurons into generated harmonics with explicit amplitudes and phases.
Seeds many low frequencies and a grid of high frequencies to cover a band efficiently.
Clamps hidden weights differently for low- and high-frequency input columns.
Uses tanh-scaled trainable column limits with magnitude regularization.
Tests whether image fitting preserves derivatives without derivative supervision.

evaluations.setting: Kodak images with 90% observed pixels and 10% held out, sinusoidal MLPs trained with Adam.
evaluations.metric: Signal PSNR and analytical-gradient PSNR against a Sobel target.
evaluations.result: Structured initialization improves over uniform initialization and favors a large low-frequency allocation.
evaluations.baseline: Uniform first-layer frequency sampling and SIREN initialization.

evaluations.setting: Fixed-bound and no-bound training across multiple frequency thresholds.
evaluations.result: Bounds improve the signal in every reported setting and gradient PSNR by 9.6 dB on average.
evaluations.baseline: Identical network trained without hidden-weight bounds.

evaluations.setting: SIREN, BACON, and TUNER across three architectures and bandlimits 85, 171, and 256.
evaluations.metric: Train/test signal and gradient PSNR plus convergence plots.
evaluations.result: TUNER is consistently more robust at high thresholds and usually gives the best signal reconstruction; gradient ordering is more mixed against BACON.

evaluations.setting: Approximately 67K-parameter BACON, BANF, and TUNER at bandlimits 60 and 130.
evaluations.result: TUNER avoids the reported BACON ringing and BANF edge distortions in the shown examples.
evaluations.baseline: BACON hard spectral filter and BANF grid-based filter.

limitations: Main experiments are image fitting; audio, SDF, radiance-field, and PDE claims are not tested.
The main analysis and experiments emphasize one hidden sinusoidal layer; deeper-network expansion is supplementary and lightly evaluated.
A target bandlimit or Nyquist bound and several sampling/bounding hyperparameters must still be chosen.
Freezing integer first-layer frequencies imposes periodic structure that may not suit nonperiodic or irregular domains.
Gradient PSNR uses a Sobel-derived target rather than exact underlying continuous derivatives.
Most comparisons use one dataset family and may depend on parameter matching and method-specific tuning.
The amplitude upper bound can be loose and does not alone give an exact compact spectral cutoff.
failure_modes: Too many high input frequencies produce noisy held-out pixels and derivatives.
Bounds that are too tight underfit legitimate detail, while loose or unregularized learned bounds permit spectral leakage.
Omitting coordinate unit frequencies can create sub-periodic reconstructions.
A mistaken bandlimit can bias the representation even when training is stable.
Hard comparison filters can ring, while soft amplitude suppression can blur high-frequency detail.
reusable_insights: Analyze the frequencies created by layer composition, not only those explicitly initialized in the first layer.
Evaluate derivative fidelity on unsupervised points to distinguish accurate interpolation from high-frequency memorization.
Associate constraints with frequency groups so regularization can be stronger where spectral leakage is most likely.
A soft spectral prior can be preferable to hard truncation when ringing artifacts matter.
open_questions: Can the learned bounds be calibrated from data without a known bandlimit?
How tight are the amplitude bounds for trained deep sinusoidal networks?
Does TUNER improve SDF normals, NeRF aliasing, audio derivatives, and physics losses under controlled benchmarks?
Can nonperiodic bases or localized atoms extend the method to irregular domains?
What is the compute-quality tradeoff relative to FINER, WIRE, hash grids, and multiresolution neural fields?
Can spectral leakage be certified directly rather than inferred from PSNR and visual spectra?

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Neural Representations with Periodic Activation Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: SIREN introduces trainable sine networks and a stable activation-statistics initialization across many signal types; TUNER derives a frequency-combination expansion and constrains hidden weights throughout training for spectral control.

competitive_landscape.title: BACON: Band-limited Coordinate Networks for Multiscale Scene Representation
competitive_landscape.difference: BACON builds an analytically band-limited multiplicative-filter architecture with multiscale outputs; TUNER retains sinusoidal MLP nonlinearities and uses soft amplitude suppression, trading exact architectural filtering for flexibility.

competitive_landscape.title: BANF: Band-limited Neural Fields for Levels of Detail Reconstruction
competitive_landscape.difference: BANF obtains low-pass neural fields through a grid-linked architectural modification for level-of-detail reconstruction; TUNER constrains the generated spectrum of coordinate MLPs via hidden-weight bounds.

competitive_landscape.title: FINER: Flexible spectral-bias tuning in Implicit NEural Representation by Variable-periodic Activation Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: FINER changes the activation and bias range to tune supported frequencies across images, SDFs, and NeRFs; TUNER keeps sine activations and explicitly samples and bounds frequency-generating parameters.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The amplitude-phase expansion supplies the first theoretically grounded joint initialization and bandlimit-control scheme for sinusoidal MLP training.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Two expansion/bound theorems motivate a low/high frequency sampler, fixed and learned hidden-column bounds, and image experiments showing improved convergence and derivative fidelity.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The explicit bridge from layer-composition algebra to a practical training constraint is distinctive. The evidence is strong for the tested shallow image-fitting regime but insufficient for broad claims about all sinusoidal neural fields or exact bandlimiting.

reviewer_notes: Read all 20 extracted pages, including theorem proofs, deeper-network extension, initialization ablations, fixed/learned bounds, and supplementary comparisons with BANF, FINER, and Fourier features. Current primary competitor records were checked on arXiv on 2026-08-23.
